section_summary: This section records disagreements among State, Labor, the Army, and SCAP over Japanese government workers’ bargaining rights, Communist influence in trade unions, and an Australian proposal before the Far Eastern Commission. It includes John W. Gibson’s recommendations, unemployment estimates, a Japanese union’s petition about police surveillance, and a despatch on a Japanese Supreme Court labor ruling. The section ends during an enclosure presenting the employer’s appeal in that case.

subfiles.title: Discussion of a proposed U.S. labor mission to Japan
subfiles.about: Officials weigh a labor mission against MacArthur’s and Dodge’s objections.
subfiles.summary: State considers labor advisers sent through the Army as a quieter response to Communist influence in Japanese unions.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Gibson’s report on Japanese labor
subfiles.about: The Labor Secretary forwards Gibson’s report and endorses its recommendations.
subfiles.summary: Tobin urges serious consideration of Gibson’s recommendations.

subfiles.title: Report of John W. Gibson, Assistant Secretary of Labor
subfiles.about: Gibson recommends changes to Japanese labor law and stronger support for democratic unions.
subfiles.summary: Gibson proposes bargaining rights for communications workers, flexible wage controls, a shorter government workweek, and a minimum wage. He also urges action against Communist union leadership, U.S. labor visits to Japan, and exchanges for Japanese unionists.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about handling Tobin’s letter and Gibson’s recommendations
subfiles.about: Butterworth asks what action has followed the Labor Department’s letter.
subfiles.summary: Requests the letter’s status, SCAP’s views, and a proposed response.

subfiles.title: Routing note to Webb concerning Gibson
subfiles.about: Butterworth forwards a memorandum questioning assurances Gibson believed he had received from SCAP.
subfiles.summary: Alerts Webb to doubts about Gibson’s reported assurances.

subfiles.title: Australian labor proposal and sodium anhydride inspection
subfiles.about: U.S. and Australian officials discuss an FEC proposal on Japanese government workers.
subfiles.summary: Allison warns Bullock that adopting Australia’s labor proposal would repudiate SCAP and might provoke unrest. Bullock explains Australia’s wish to counter Soviet proposals; they discuss possible consultation instead. Allison also confirms arrangements for an Australian inspection of a Japanese sodium anhydride process.

subfiles.title: Army transmittal of SCAP unemployment figures
subfiles.about: West confirms delivery of SCAP’s reply on Japanese unemployment.
subfiles.summary: Notes that SCAP’s unemployment reply was sent to State on April 13.

subfiles.title: SCAP estimates of Japanese unemployment
subfiles.about: SCAP estimates unemployment and describes possible relief measures.
subfiles.summary: SCAP estimates 500,000 to one million people currently unemployed and expects a smaller rise than Japan’s Labor Ministry forecasts. It discusses the stabilization program’s effects, public works, unemployment insurance, employment offices, and limits on moving workers between regions.

subfiles.title: Army position on the Australian FEC resolution
subfiles.about: West conveys Army support for SCAP’s opposition to the Australian resolution.
subfiles.summary: Urges withdrawal or tabling of the proposal and a U.S. veto if necessary.

subfiles.title: Draft reply to West on government workers’ rights
subfiles.about: State drafts a response to the Army’s position on the Australian proposal.
subfiles.summary: Seeks ways to settle the continuing dispute over National Public Service legislation.

subfiles.title: Handwritten note on decentralizing labor administration
subfiles.about: The note describes opposition to a proposed decentralization of Japanese labor administration.
subfiles.summary: It recounts Killen’s request for materials, State and Labor opposition to the proposal, and Sullivan’s expectation that their messages would strengthen SCAP’s Labor Division.

subfiles.title: State reply to West on the Australian proposal
subfiles.about: Butterworth seeks an enduring solution to the government workers’ rights dispute.
subfiles.summary: State will seek withdrawal of the proposal but asks Army how to settle the underlying controversy.

subfiles.title: Inviting Japanese unions to a new non-Communist labor international
subfiles.about: Ross and Sullivan discuss invitations to Japanese and Korean unions for Geneva meetings.
subfiles.summary: Sullivan favors contact with non-Communist Japanese unions but expects SCAP to deny attendance. Ross suggests informal contact with a Japanese worker attending the ILO meeting.

subfiles.title: Labor policy for Japan
subfiles.about: The memorandum urges a coordinated change in U.S. labor policy toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: It reviews Gibson’s proposals and SCAP’s refusals to expand telecommunications workers’ rights or permit greater international union contact. It recommends amending the National Public Service Law, enabling contacts with democratic unions abroad, adding labor specialists to SCAP, and seeking high level U.S. support.

subfiles.title: Australian resolution on Japanese government workers’ rights
subfiles.about: A cover memorandum explains the pending Australian resolution and possible U.S. veto.
subfiles.summary: Outlines the diplomatic difficulty and introduces arguments for withdrawing or tabling the resolution.

subfiles.title: Arguments against the Australian labor resolution
subfiles.about: The memorandum sets out arguments for persuading Australia to withdraw its FEC proposal.
subfiles.summary: It argues that the resolution would undermine SCAP, destabilize Japanese politics, and transfer responsibility for banning strikes to the occupation authority. It favors consultation on changes to Japanese legislation.

subfiles.title: Thorp’s response on the Australian resolution
subfiles.about: Thorp proposes a U.S. commitment to bargaining rights as a way to resolve the FEC dispute.
subfiles.summary: Thorp supports opposing the Australian text but doubts it can be withdrawn without assurances of U.S. action. He urges bargaining, mediation, and arbitration rights for non-executive government enterprise workers, with Cabinet or White House intervention if SCAP continues to object.

subfiles.title: Notice of Chester W. Hepler’s Washington visit
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; Departments of State and Labor
subfiles.about: SCAP announces Hepler’s travel and requests meetings on Japanese labor issues.
subfiles.summary: Provides Hepler’s travel dates and asks interested agencies to arrange conferences.

subfiles.title: United Metal Workers of Japan petition to President Truman
subfiles.from: Jiro Ide, United Metal Workers of Japan
subfiles.about: The union protests police attendance and note-taking at its Tokyo congress.
subfiles.summary: The petition says a police officer claimed to act at the request of occupation authorities when entering the May 31 congress. It asks Truman to consider whether such surveillance violates workers’ freedom of speech and assembly.

subfiles.title: Bishop’s objections to escalating the Australian resolution
subfiles.about: Bishop opposes Cabinet intervention to reverse SCAP’s decision.
subfiles.summary: He favors urging FEC partners to withdraw or table the resolution and using a veto if necessary.

subfiles.title: Proposed U.S. course on government enterprise workers’ rights
subfiles.about: Butterworth recommends a high level U.S. position on bargaining rights and the Australian FEC resolution.
subfiles.summary: The draft seeks Cabinet level agreement that non-executive government enterprise workers should receive collective bargaining, mediation, and arbitration rights without a right to strike. It proposes asking Commonwealth delegations to delay a vote while the United States develops its position. It examines SCAP’s exclusion of telecommunications workers and the diplomatic costs of either adopting the Australian text or vetoing it.

subfiles.title: Japanese Supreme Court labor decision
subfiles.from: Cloyce K. Huston, U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch reports a Supreme Court ruling against a mining company president for penalizing union members.
subfiles.summary: Huston recounts the strike, Shigemori’s suspensions and dismissals, and the Court’s April 23 rejection of his appeal. The ruling treats retaliatory suspension, including suspension with pay, as potentially injurious treatment under labor law.

subfiles.title: Hiroshima Higher Court decision: facts of the Shigemori case
subfiles.doc_type: translated court decision excerpt; despatch enclosure 1
subfiles.about: The excerpt recounts the strike and the employer’s disciplinary actions.
subfiles.summary: It describes wage demands, a strike, its settlement, and Shigemori’s subsequent suspension and discharge of miners and supporting office employees. The court characterizes the discipline as intended to weaken the unions.

subfiles.title: Summary of Shigemori’s appeal to the Supreme Court
subfiles.from: Keuke Nobuo and Hirosawa Michihiko, attorneys for Goroku Shigemori
subfiles.about: Shigemori’s lawyers challenge findings that his suspensions and dismissals unlawfully harmed union members.
subfiles.summary: The lawyers argue that workers engaged in organized slowdowns after the strike was settled and that discipline addressed misconduct rather than union activity. They contest the lower court’s findings about motive, the office employees, the union’s aims, and the meaning of injurious treatment. Their sixth argument continues beyond page 214.
